Fichte

Johann Gottlieb Fichte (1762–1814) radicalized the Kantian program: the ego does not merely structure experience—it posits both itself and the not-self (the world) through its own activity 1. The world model, on this view, is not imposed on a passively received sensory stream; it is spontaneously generated by the agent itself. This emphasis on the constitutive activity of the subject resonates with active inference, where the organism enacts its world through the interplay of prediction and action. This historical source image illustrates the period (Figure).

Hegel

G.W.F. Hegel (1770–1831) described consciousness as a developmental process in the Phenomenology of Spirit 2. Each stage of awareness—from raw sensory certainty through perception, understanding, self-consciousness, and onward—discovers the inadequacy of its current model and is driven, through contradiction, to a richer one. The result is a dialectical, self-correcting hierarchy of representations, making Hegel an unexpected precursor to iterative, hierarchical inference. This historical source image illustrates the period (Figure).

Schopenhauer

Arthur Schopenhauer (1788–1860) opened The World as Will and Representation 3 with a sentence that could serve as an epigraph for this book: “The world is my representation.” Everything we experience—objects, space, time, causality—is the brain’s representational construction. Behind the representation lies the blind, purposeless Will (the thing-in-itself), forever inaccessible to the modeling apparatus. Schopenhauer thus articulated, more starkly than any predecessor, the condition of an organism that can never step outside its own world model.

Herbart

Johann Friedrich Herbart (1776–1841) was the first to insist that psychology must be a mathematical science 4. Ideas have quantitative strengths; they compete for access to consciousness, with weaker ideas being inhibited below a threshold (the Schwelle). His “statics and mechanics of mind”—systems of differential equations governing the rise and fall of ideas through mutual inhibition and reinforcement—constitute a remarkably early neural-network-like dynamics of mental representation.

Lotze

Hermann Lotze (1817–1881) addressed a puzzle that remains central to computational neuroscience: how does the brain construct spatial perception from non-spatial neural signals 5, 6? His theory of local signs (Localzeichen) proposed that each retinal point contributes a qualitatively distinct signal; spatial layout is then reconstructed by learning the lawful relationships among these signals and their motor consequences. This is the insight that the brain must decode its own neural code—that representation and the interpretation of representation are equally necessary.

Johannes Müller (1801–1858) established the law of specific nerve energies: each sensory nerve, regardless of how it is stimulated, produces only its own characteristic quality of sensation 7. Press on the closed eye and you see flashes of light, not pressure; electrically stimulate the auditory nerve and you hear a tone, not a tingle. The implication is profound and extends Kant’s philosophy into physiology: the brain has no direct access to the external world—it receives only the qualitatively idiosyncratic signals of its own nerves, and the character of experience is determined by which nerve fires, not by the physical nature of the external stimulus. Müller thus provided the physiological bridge between Kant’s claim that the mind imposes form on experience and Helmholtz’s subsequent theory of perception as unconscious inference: if all the brain ever receives is its own neural activity, then the perception of a coherent world “out there” must be a construction.

Maine de Biran

Maine de Biran (1766–1824) argued that the most fundamental datum of consciousness is not passive sensation but effort—the volitional, motor sense of exerting force against bodily and environmental resistance 8, 9. The self is not discovered through Cartesian meditation on thought but through the lived experience of willed bodily action: I move, therefore I am. Furthermore, habit progressively automates what was once effortful, transforming deliberate voluntary acts into transparent, nearly reflexive operations that withdraw from conscious awareness. For active inference, Maine de Biran is a remarkable precursor: his insistence that the self is constituted through motor engagement with the world, and that consciousness emerges precisely where prediction meets resistance, anticipates the primacy of action in the free energy framework.
